title: Regular verbs: -ar, -er, -ir
description: Conjugate everyday -ar, -er and -ir verbs in the present and use gostar de.

guide.summary: Brazilian Portuguese verbs fall into three families by their infinitive: -ar, -er and -ir. Each family cuts off its ending and adds a short set of new ones, and because você, ele, ela and a gente share one form, and vocês, eles and elas share another, you only need four forms per verb. This page has the three families, the shared forms, the nós endings, what the present is used for, and gostar de.

sections.title: -ar verbs: falar
sections.text: Most verbs end in -ar. Remove -ar to get the stem (fal-) and add -o, -a, -amos or -am. The a of the infinitive comes back in every form except eu.
steps: Find the subject: who is doing it?
Remove -ar to get the stem.
Add the ending on that subject’s row: -o, -a, -amos or -am.
watch: The eu form ends in -o in all three families, never in -a.
A noun subject counts as ele or eles: a Maria fala, meus pais falam.

sections.title: -er verbs: comer
sections.text: For -er verbs remove -er and add -o, -e, -emos or -em. The pattern is the -ar one with e in place of a.
steps: Check that the infinitive ends in -er.
Remove -er to get the stem.
Add -o, -e, -emos or -em: e replaces the a of the -ar endings.

examples.pt: Eu como pão no café da manhã.

examples.en: They sell fruit at the market.

watch: Do not borrow the -ar vowel: ele come, not ele coma.
Ler, ter, fazer and a few others end in -er but are irregular; they have their own topic.

sections.title: -ir verbs: abrir, partir
sections.text: -ir verbs share the -er endings in three forms: -o, -e and -em. Only nós is different: it keeps the i of the infinitive, -imos.
steps: Check that the infinitive ends in -ir.
Remove -ir and add -o, -e or -em, exactly as for -er verbs.
For nós write -imos, never -emos.

examples.pt: Eu abro a janela de manhã.
examples.en: I open the window in the morning.

watch: Ele abre, not ele abri: the i appears only in the infinitive and in nós.
Partir means to leave or set off; in everyday speech Brazilians often say sair instead.

sections.title: Who shares a form
sections.text: Brazilians say você for you, and você takes the same form as ele and ela. A gente, the everyday way to say we, also takes that form. In the plural, vocês, eles and elas share one form. Tu exists in some regions, such as the South and parts of the North and Northeast, often with the você form of the verb (tu fala); you will hear it, but this course uses você.
steps: Is the subject one person, you or a gente? Use the singular form ending in a vowel.
Is it several people, including vocês? Add -m to that form.
A noun counts too: a Maria takes the singular form, meus pais the plural.

examples.pt: A gente come em casa no domingo.
examples.en: We eat at home on Sunday.

watch: A gente means we but takes the ele form: a gente fala, not a gente falamos.
Você is grammatically like ele, even though it means you.

sections.title: The nós forms: -amos, -emos, -imos
sections.text: The nós ending is the infinitive vowel plus -mos. So the infinitive tells you which one to use.
steps: Look at the vowel before the final r of the infinitive.
Keep that vowel and add -mos.
The subject nós is often dropped: the -mos already says who.
watch: In speech a gente is more common than nós, but you need to recognise and write both.

sections.title: What the present is for
sections.text: The simple present covers habits and facts, and also plans that are already fixed, usually with a time word such as amanhã or no sábado. English often uses I am working or I work in these places; Portuguese just uses the simple present.
steps: Is it a habit, a general fact or a fixed plan? Use the simple present.
For a plan, add the time word: amanhã, no sábado, hoje à noite.
Keep estar plus an -ndo form for what is happening right now.

examples.pt: Ela corre na praia todo dia.
examples.en: She runs on the beach every day.

watch: For I am working tomorrow, Portuguese does not need the -ndo form: eu trabalho amanhã or eu vou trabalhar amanhã.
Ir plus an infinitive also talks about the future; the simple present sounds more settled.

sections.title: Gostar de
sections.text: Gostar is a regular -ar verb, but it always needs de before what you like, whether that is a noun or another verb in the infinitive.

rows: a noun with o or a

steps: Conjugate gostar like falar: gosto, gosta, gostamos, gostam.
Put de straight after it.
If the thing has o or a in front, de joins it: do, da, dos, das.
watch: English like has no preposition; gostar never works without de.
The verb after de stays in the infinitive: ela gosta de cozinhar, not ela gosta de cozinha.

steps: Find the subject.
Remove -ar from the infinitive.
Add -o, -a, -amos or -am for that subject.
Check the infinitive ends in -er.
Remove -er.
Add -o, -e, -emos or -em for that subject.
Check the infinitive ends in -ir.
Use -o, -e or -em as for -er verbs.
Only nós is different: -imos.
One person, você or a gente: the singular form ending in a vowel.
Several people, vocês included: add -m.
Find the vowel before the final r of the infinitive.
Keep it and add -mos.
Habit, fact or fixed plan: simple present.
For a plan, keep the time word that says when.
Conjugate gostar like falar.
Put de after it, before the noun or infinitive.
de plus o or a becomes do or da.
